_comment: English descriptions for the IBA classics — the canonical source layer. One or two sentences, 90-160 characters. They say how a drink tastes or what makes it work, allow one concrete fact where it is defensible, and never restate the ingredient list that sits twenty pixels below. No exclamation marks, no 'must-try'.
alexander: Dessert in a coupe: cream and cacao rounded off by brandy, with grated nutmeg doing more work than it looks.
americano: The Negroni's lighter ancestor. Soda stretches the Campari and vermouth into something you can drink before dinner rather than after.
angel-face: Three spirits in equal measure and no citrus at all, which is why it drinks softer and heavier than it reads.
aviation: Maraschino and violet turn a gin sour pale blue-grey. Restraint matters — a heavy hand on the violette makes it taste of soap.
bee-s-knees: A Prohibition drink built to hide rough gin behind honey. The honey has to be thinned to syrup first or it seizes in the shaker.
bellini: Venice, 1948, and named after a painter's pink. White peach only: yellow peach turns it cloying.
between-the-sheets: A Sidecar with rum added, which sounds like too much and is not. Drier and sharper than either drink alone.
black-russian: Two ingredients over ice. Everything depends on the coffee liqueur, since there is nothing to hide behind.
bloody-mary: The savoury cocktail. Roll it between two glasses rather than shaking, or the tomato juice goes thin and frothy.
boulevardier: A Negroni that swaps gin for whiskey. Warmer, rounder, and better suited to a cold evening than the original.
bramble: A gin sour with blackberry liqueur trailed through it after building, so the drink bleeds red from the bottom up.
brandy-crusta: The ancestor of the Sidecar, and the drink that introduced the sugared rim. The lemon peel lines the whole glass.
caipirinha: Brazil's national drink. Muddle the lime skin-down so the oil comes out of the peel and not just the juice.
canchanchara: Cuban, and older than the Daiquiri. Honey and lime over aguardiente, cut with water rather than shaken.
cardinale: A drier Negroni: dry vermouth instead of sweet. Sharper and more bitter, with none of the original's roundness.
casino: A pre-Prohibition gin sour, dry and slightly nutty from the maraschino, with orange bitters lifting the finish.
champagne-cocktail: A sugar cube soaked in bitters, dropped into champagne. It keeps releasing bubbles from the bottom the whole way down.
chartreuse-swizzle: Swizzled until the glass frosts. Chartreuse carries 130 herbs, and pineapple is one of the few things that can stand up to it.
clover-club: A raspberry gin sour with an egg-white head. Dry-shake first or the foam never sets properly.
corpse-reviver-2: A morning-after drink from the 1930s, and genuinely bracing. The absinthe is a rinse, not a measure.
cosmopolitan: Tarter than its reputation. The cranberry is there for colour and edge, not sweetness — this is a citrus drink.
cuba-libre: Rum and cola only becomes this when the lime goes in. Squeeze it in and drop the shell in the glass.
daiquiri: Three ingredients and nowhere to hide. Get the balance of lime and sugar right and it is the best test of a bar there is.
dark-n-stormy: Poured, not stirred, so the dark rum sits as a layer on the ginger beer. The name is trademarked in Bermuda.
don-s-special-daiquiri: A tiki blend from Don the Beachcomber, richer than a Daiquiri and thicker, with passion fruit doing the lifting.
dry-martini: Two ingredients, endlessly argued about. Stirred, never shaken — shaking clouds it and bruises the vermouth.
espresso-martini: Invented in 1980s London for a guest who wanted something to wake her up. Only fresh espresso gives it the crema.
fernandito: Argentina drinks more Fernet than anywhere else, mostly like this. Bitter, medicinal, and oddly refreshing over ice.
french-75: Named after a field gun for the kick. Gin and lemon under champagne, and it hits harder than it tastes.
french-connection: Two ingredients, no dilution beyond the ice. Amaretto rounds the cognac without covering it.
french-martini: Not a Martini at all. Pineapple juice shaken hard gives it the foam that makes it look like one.
garibaldi: Campari and orange juice, but the juice must be fluffy — whipped, not poured — or it is just bitter and flat.
gin-basil-smash: A Hamburg invention from 2008 and already a modern standard. Smash the basil once, hard; shredding it turns the drink bitter.
gin-fizz: A sour lengthened with soda. Serve it without ice in the glass so the head stays intact.
grand-margarita: A Margarita made richer with Grand Marnier in place of triple sec. Rounder, with more orange and less bite.
grasshopper: Mint and chocolate in cream, and unapologetically a dessert. Serves better after a meal than during one.
hanky-panky: Created by Ada Coleman at the Savoy for an actor who wanted something with a kick. Fernet is the whole point.
hemingway-special: Grapefruit and maraschino, and no sugar at all — Hemingway asked for double rum and none. Dry and bracing.
horse-s-neck: The garnish is the drink's name: one unbroken spiral of lemon peel hung over the rim, running the length of the glass.
iba-tiki: A modern tiki build with two rums and a nut liqueur. Complex, sweet, and much stronger than it presents.
illegal: Mezcal and overproof rum, smoky and sharp at once. The falernum keeps the two from fighting each other.
irish-coffee: Hot coffee under cold cream, and never stirred — you drink one through the other. Whip the cream just to the point it pours.
john-collins: A Tom Collins made with dry gin. Built in the glass rather than shaken, so it stays clear and lightly carbonated.
jungle-bird: Campari in a tiki drink, which should not work. Pineapple and blackstrap rum absorb the bitterness and it does.
kir: Burgundy's aperitif: a splash of blackcurrant in dry white wine. Named after a mayor of Dijon who served it constantly.
last-word: Equal parts, all four assertive, and somehow balanced. Lost for decades and revived in Seattle in the 2000s.
lemon-drop-martini: A sugared rim and a lemon sour underneath. Sharper than it looks if the lemon is fresh.
long-island-ice-tea: Five spirits and a splash of cola that makes it look like iced tea. Tastes of none of them individually, which is the trick.
mai-tai: Trader Vic's, 1944, and nothing to do with pineapple juice. Orgeat and lime over good rum, with a mint sprig for the nose.
manhattan: The drink that made vermouth respectable. Stirred until properly cold, and better with rye than with bourbon.
margarita: Lime and orange over tequila, salted on one half of the rim so the drinker chooses. Fresh lime or nothing.
martinez: The link between the Dry Martini and the Manhattan, and older than both. Sweeter, darker, and worth knowing.
mary-pickford: Havana in the 1920s, named for the silent-film actress. Pineapple and grenadine keep it pink and soft.
mimosa: Half orange juice, half sparkling, and the temperature matters more than the ratio. Both ingredients must be properly cold.
mint-julep: The Kentucky Derby's drink. Packed with crushed ice until the cup frosts on the outside — hold it by the rim.
missionary-s-downfall: A blended tiki drink built on mint and peach. Lighter and fresher than most of the category.
mojito: Muddle the mint gently — you want the oil, not shredded leaf, which turns bitter and leaves black flecks in the glass.
monkey-gland: Paris, 1920s, named after a discredited surgical fad. Absinthe and grenadine over gin and orange, and better than the story.
moscow-mule: Invented to sell vodka and copper mugs in equal measure. Ginger beer, not ginger ale — the heat is the point.
naked-and-famous: Equal parts, smoky and bitter at once. A modern descendant of the Last Word, built on mezcal instead of gin.
negroni: The aperitivo that taught bitterness to be charming. Stirred, never shaken — twenty seconds is the whole recipe.
new-york-sour: A whiskey sour with red wine floated on top. The wine sits in a band and mixes as you drink, changing it halfway.
old-cuban: A Mojito dressed for the evening: aged rum, bitters and champagne. Created at New York's Pegu Club in the 2000s.
old-fashioned: The original definition of a cocktail — spirit, sugar, bitters, water. Everything since is a variation on it.
paloma: Mexico drinks far more of these than Margaritas. Grapefruit soda and salt, and it works because it is not sweet.
paper-plane: Equal parts, created in 2008 and now everywhere. Two bitter amari against bourbon and lemon, and none of them wins.
paradise: An apricot gin sour from the 1920s, softer than most. The orange juice rounds the edges rather than sharpening them.
penicillin: Honey, ginger and lemon over blended Scotch, with a smoky Islay float on top so the peat hits the nose first.
pina-colada: Puerto Rico's national drink. Coconut cream, not coconut milk — the difference is the whole texture.
pisco-punch: San Francisco's Gold Rush drink, and once a closely guarded secret. Pineapple steeped in syrup is what made it famous.
pisco-sour: Peru's national drink, and the egg white is not optional — it is what turns a sharp sour into something silky.
planter-s-punch: One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak. The rhyme predates the recipe by a century.
porn-star-martini: London, 2002, and served with a shot of champagne on the side rather than in it. Alternate sips; that is the design.
porto-flip: A flip is any drink with a whole egg or yolk shaken in. This one is warming, thick, and better in winter.
rabo-de-galo: Brazilian, and the name means rooster's tail. Cachaça with vermouth and Cynar — bitter, herbal and low on sugar.
ramos-fizz: New Orleans, and famously shaken for twelve minutes in the original bar. Two minutes gets you most of the way there.
remember-the-maine: A Manhattan with cherry brandy and an absinthe rinse, named after the 1898 battleship. Rich and faintly medicinal.
russian-spring-punch: Dick Bradsell again: blackcurrant and lemon under sparkling wine, long and easy to drink for its strength.
rusty-nail: Scotch sweetened with Scotch — Drambuie is whisky, honey and herbs. Two ingredients, no citrus, no dilution.
sazerac: New Orleans' own, and the absinthe is a rinse you discard. Traditionally served with no ice at all.
sea-breeze: Cranberry and grapefruit are bitter in different directions, and the vodka simply carries them. Long and dry.
sex-on-the-beach: Peach and cranberry over vodka, and sweeter than most of this list. Built in the glass, never shaken.
sherry-cobbler: The drink that popularised the drinking straw in the 1830s. Shaken with fruit and served over a mound of crushed ice.
sidecar: Paris after the First World War. Cognac, orange and lemon in near-equal measure, with a sugared rim if you like.
singapore-sling: The Raffles Hotel, around 1915, and the recipe has been argued over ever since. Eight ingredients that somehow settle.
southside: A gin sour with mint, said to have been the drink of Chicago's South Side during Prohibition. Clean and sharp.
spicy-fifty: Chilli infused into the shake rather than the bottle, so the heat builds slowly. Elderflower keeps it floral underneath.
spritz: Venice, and the ratio is fixed: three prosecco, two Aperol, one soda. Low in alcohol and built for the afternoon.
stinger: Cognac and mint, and nothing else. Once the drink you ordered last, to clear the palate before leaving.
suffering-bastard: Cairo, 1942, invented as a hangover cure for soldiers. Ginger beer over gin and cognac, which reads worse than it drinks.
tequila-sunrise: Poured and left alone — the grenadine sinks and stays there. Stirring it destroys the only reason it has that name.
three-dots-and-a-dash: Morse code for V, for victory, and the garnish spells it out. A dense tiki blend from 1940s Chicago.
tipperary: Irish whiskey with Chartreuse, which is a strange pairing until you taste it. Herbal, sweet and quite strong.
tommy-s-margarita: San Francisco's version: agave syrup instead of orange liqueur. Cleaner, and it tastes more of the tequila.
trinidad-sour: Built on a full ounce and a half of bitters, which should be undrinkable and is not. Orgeat is what saves it.
tuxedo: A Martini with maraschino and an absinthe rinse. Older, sweeter and more aromatic than the drink it became.
ve-n-to: An IBA addition built on grappa, with chamomile and honey softening a spirit most people find sharp.
vesper: Invented in print, in Casino Royale, before anyone made one. Shaken, as specified, though it drinks better stirred.
vieux-carre: New Orleans' French Quarter in a glass, and named after it. Two spirits, two bitters, and nothing sharp anywhere.
whiskey-sour: Get the foam right and it is a different drink — an egg white is optional but transforms the texture.
white-lady: A Sidecar built on gin instead of cognac. Sharper and drier, and it needs the sugar the Sidecar can do without.
zombie: Don the Beachcomber, 1934, and famously limited to two per customer. Three rums, and the recipe was secret for decades.
